## Series Overview

Improving a segmentation model is an experiment loop: form a hypothesis, change something, train, evaluate, read the errors,
repeat. Agents can run that loop. The hard part is not running it. It is **trusting the result**, because a factory that runs
hundreds of experiments will find changes that look better on its evaluation and are not. The central question is how to
build a model factory whose improvements are real, and whether it beats a plain search at the same cost.

**Why this matters for the inspection system.** In
[Part 7 of Zero to Advanced](../agentic-zero-to-advanced/07-the-inspection-pipeline.qmd) the whole pipeline turned out to be
capped by its detector: the classical detector proposed a box for only 11 of the 125 real defects on the held-out frames, so
nothing downstream could find the rest. A better segmentation model is the lever, and this factory is how I plan to build one.

**What changes compared with the software factory.** The artifact is a trained model, not a code change. A ticket is a
hypothesis ("heavier augmentation on thin voids will raise recall") with a GPU budget and an expected effect. The gate is a
locked evaluator. And "robust" is defined before any score is seen.

**The spine of the series: evaluate, analyse, recommend.** The factory does not just try things. After every evaluation it
does an **error analysis** (what kinds of mistakes: missed defects, false alarms, merged or split regions, wrong boundaries)
and a **slice analysis** (where does the model fail: which sizes, contrasts, noise levels, backgrounds), and then writes a
**recommendation** for a better model: more real data of a specific kind, targeted new synthetic data, a model or training
change, label fixes, or "leave it". Each recommendation carries its evidence (the slice table with counts and intervals) and
a predicted effect, and it is then tried as an experiment. A recommendation that does not hold up is recorded as wrong.

**The loop, run more than once.** Find the weakness, name a possible fix, try it, look at the result, and go round again with
the next weakness. A typical round: a slice is bad because it has very little data. The recommendation is targeted synthetic
data for that slice. The factory adds it, retrains, and checks whether the **real** slice improved. Each round is logged as
weakness, fix tried and result, including the rounds where the fix did nothing or made it worse.

**Synthetic data is an art, so it gets checked.** Making synthetic images is easy. Knowing whether they are realistic enough
to be useful is the hard part, and "looks real" is not the same as "helps". So the series checks the synthetic data directly
(do its statistics match real images, can a classifier or a person tell them apart) and, more importantly, by what it does
downstream on real data.

**Data curation, at two levels.** Before and between experiments the factory curates the training data, and curation works at
two different levels:

- **Whole-image curation.** Which images are in the set at all: exact and near-duplicate images removed (and overlapping tiles
  cut from the same source), bad acquisitions filtered out
  (blank, saturated, artefact-ridden), coverage across acquisition conditions checked, hard images found, and splits kept
  free of near-duplicates of each other so nothing leaks from training into the test sets.
- **Defect-mask curation.** What is inside the masks: **duplicate defects** (the same physical defect appearing in overlapping
  tiles or repeated frames, or near-identical masks from a generator with too little variety), the distribution of defect sizes, contrasts and shapes, badly drawn or
  inconsistent masks, suspected label errors (a person decides), rare defect types, and how defects are sampled, for example
  crops centred on defects instead of whole images.

Curation is also one of the actions the factory can recommend ("remove these 40 near-duplicates", "re-draw these masks",
"oversample thin voids"). Like every other fix, it is tested against a plain control: a random subset of the same size.

## What the research found, and what it changed

- **Plain search is a serious competitor.** In published comparisons I could open, classical hyperparameter optimisation
  matched or beat an LLM agent inside a fixed search space, and agents were competitive mainly when they could edit code. One of
  those studies found an agent's early lead came from a default configuration it was seeded with
  ([Ferreira et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.24647v2), which has internal inconsistencies and leaves LLM inference time out
  of the budget; [a budget-matched tabular study](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.21641)). I found no equal-compute comparison of a
  full ML-engineering agent against a plain sweep, so this series will run one.
- **Agents overfit the evaluation they can see.** In AIRA-dsl, choosing the final candidate by test score instead of validation
  score changed the medal rate by 9 to 13 points ([AIRA-dsl](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.02554)). On the other side, one 2026
  paper found little adaptive-overfitting risk under coarse feedback on 8 datasets (abstract read only)
  ([arXiv 2606.11045](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11045)). So the honest position is that the effect size depends on the setup,
  and this series will measure it instead of assuming it.
- **A held-out set can be queried too often.** The reusable-holdout work shows how many queries a test set survives, and the
  Ladder shows the leak even from a scalar score ([Thresholdout](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.02629.pdf),
  [Ladder](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)). Across more than 100 Kaggle competitions overfitting was small (typically under
  1%), except where the test sets had only 90 to 209 examples; the authors suggest at least 10,000 examples
  ([Roelofs et al.](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2019/file/ee39e503b6bedf0c98c388b7e8589aca-Paper.pdf)). That is far
  more than tens of positives, which is why the sealed set here has to be large, and therefore synthetic.
- **No published definition of a "false-win rate" exists.** I will define one in the posts (below) and say that it is my
  definition.
- **Agents tamper when they can.** The same evidence as in the software-factory series applies: an agent that can read or
  write the evaluator will use it, and prompts are not a control. The same gate design is reused here.
- **I have not yet researched the error-analysis side.** My research pass covered factories, ML-engineering agents, evaluation
  overfitting, robustness metrics, datasets and sandboxing. It did not cover slice-discovery methods, learning-curve
  extrapolation, or methods for judging how realistic synthetic images are (statistical comparison, two-sample tests,
  train-on-synthetic and test-on-real), or for curation (near-duplicate detection, diversity and core-set selection; I did look at
  confident-learning methods for label errors), so the posts on those parts will start with a reading pass before I plan them in detail.
- **I found no X-ray or segmentation factory studies,** and no published agent for finding label errors in segmentation masks.
  The closest segmentation-agent paper I found (Camyla) I read at abstract level only, so I am not building on its claims.

## The design rules

1. **Three evaluation tiers.** An open development set, a locked confirmation set that answers only "better than the current best
   by more than a margin" at coarse precision, and a final sealed set touched once per milestone. Plus a second set that is never
   queried, to detect leakage.
2. **A locked evaluator** that agents cannot edit, running in a separate process from a pinned copy, with the sealed labels never
   mounted into the agents' environment. Sandbox, permissions and audit log are the shared factory core from the software
   factory series.
3. **An honest control.** A TPE or random search over the same architecture's hyperparameters, seeded with the same default
   configuration, with the same data, evaluator and equal GPU-hours, plus a second agent arm that may edit code. LLM tokens and time
   are reported separately.
4. **Pre-registered decisions.** The rule for calling a result a win is written down before the run.
5. **Leakage checks** on every experiment (is a test image in the training data, did a label change).
6. **Humans in the loop for labels.** Agents may find suspected label errors. A person decides.
7. **Slices are found on one set and confirmed on another.** Scanning many slices for failures is itself a selection effect: look
   at enough of them and some will look bad by chance. So slice findings carry counts and intervals, tiny slices are not
   reported, and a finding has to reproduce on data that was not used to find it.
8. **Synthetic data is judged by what it does on real data,** not by how real it looks. Realism checks are reported, but the test
   that counts is whether a real held-out slice improves, against a plain-augmentation control with the same number of added
   examples. Realism metrics can be good while the data still teaches the model the wrong thing, or bad while it still helps.
9. **Curation, deduplication included, is judged against random selection.** A curated subset has to beat a random subset of the
   same size (and removing duplicates against removing the same number of random items), and curation may
   only touch the evaluation sets to remove leakage, with every such change logged. Otherwise "cleaner data" is a story, not a result.
10. **A recommendation must be falsifiable.** It states the evidence, the action and the effect it predicts. The factory then runs
   the action. If the sealed score does not move as predicted, the recommendation counts as wrong.

**Defining the false-win rate (my definition, not a published one).** A run is a *win* if it beats the current best on development
data by the pre-registered rule. It is a *false win* if its paired difference on the sealed set is not positive, or its interval
falls below a margin. The false-win rate is false wins divided by wins, with a Wilson or Clopper-Pearson interval. To get a
baseline, an A/A experiment sends the same configuration with different seeds, and no-op code edits, through the identical
pipeline, so any "wins" are false by construction.

## Data and licensing

No company data goes into this series, and the main dataset will be synthetic.

- GDXray, which the earlier series first used, is offered for research and educational use only, with redistribution and commercial use
  prohibited, and its annotations are mostly boxes and image labels, not pixel masks
  ([GDXray page](https://domingomery.ing.uc.cl/material/gdxray)). Those posts were rebuilt on this series' synthetic dataset.
- My search found no radiographic defect dataset with pixel masks and a clearly permissive licence. I checked the candidates at their
  sources: the Apache-2.0 weld-seam set on Zenodo turns out to be a text-recognition dataset (images paired with ID strings, no
  defects and no masks), so it is no use here. MVTec AD (real defect masks, plus defect-free images) and KolektorSDD2 (surface
  defects) are both CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: non-commercial and share-alike. The Magnetic Tile defect set states no licence at all.
- So the plan is to generate **my own synthetic voids with exact masks** and release the generator. The first version exists and is described
  in [post 1](01-synthetic-void-dataset.qmd): Fashion-MNIST silhouettes as parts, simulated X-ray attenuation and drawn voids, which avoids the image-licence
  problem entirely and makes a large sealed set cheap. Real data is used only locally as a sim-to-real check and never shown.
- The cost is stated up front: synthetic data cannot test real distribution shift, and published work finds that models trained only
  on simulated X-rays often fail on real ones
  ([wheel X-ray study](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.19175v1)).

## Planned measures

Decided before building, published whatever they turn out to be:

- the **recommendation hit rate**: how often following a recommendation improves the sealed worst-slice score beyond noise,
  against a default action at the same cost
- on synthetic data, where I can plant a known cause (remove a size range from training, add label noise, shrink the model),
  whether the analysis names that cause
- how real the synthetic data is: how well a classifier separates real from synthetic images, how often a person does, and how
  its size, contrast and noise statistics compare with real images
- curated against random subsets of the same size, at the image level and at the defect level, on the sealed worst-slice score
- the gain on a **real** slice from a synthetic top-up, against plain augmentation with the same number of examples, and against
  adding nothing
- the **false-win rate**, from the A/A experiment and from replaying wins against the sealed set
- the gap between the queried and never-queried sets
- the best sealed-set robustness score at equal GPU-hours, agents against the plain sweep, over three or more seeds
- human minutes per reviewed image, and how many suspected label errors a person confirms

## Posts in this Series (all coming soon)

Each post will end with a "what I did not do" section. The outcomes below are open questions, not promises.

1. **[A synthetic void dataset with exact masks](01-synthetic-void-dataset.qmd)** (written). Fashion-MNIST silhouettes as parts, simulated X-ray attenuation, and parametric voids (size, count, contrast, noise, thickness, background) with
   metadata for slicing, with checks on the masks, the splits and the contrast range, and a plain list of what is unrealistic about it.
2. **How real is the synthetic data?** Compare size, contrast, noise and edge statistics against real images, try to tell real from
   synthetic with a classifier, and with a blind test on a person, and then show why none of that is enough: the real test is use.
   Report the realism gaps I find, and what they probably mean for the later posts.
3. **Metrics that do not hide tiny voids, and a robustness suite.** Defect-level recall and precision by connected component,
   recall by size bin, boundary IoU, bootstrap over images (my recommendation, not a cited standard), plus about six
   X-ray-plausible perturbations at five severities. Show a case where pixel recall is high and object recall is low. I found no
   published X-ray corruption suite, so that part is my design.
4. **Sealing the test set and locking the evaluator.** The three tiers behind the shared gate runner. Run a boosting-style attack
   on a naive evaluator that returns scores, to show the leak, and report the queried against never-queried gap.
5. **Data curation, part 1: whole images.** Deduplication first: exact duplicates by hashing, near-duplicates by embedding
   similarity, and overlapping tiles traced back to their source image. Then quality filters, coverage across conditions,
   hard-image mining, and split hygiene (no near-duplicates across training, validation and test). The similarity threshold is a
   judgement call, so the post shows how the results move as it changes. Train on the curated set and on a random subset of the
   same size, and report the difference, including when there is none.
6. **Data curation, part 2: defect masks.** Deduplication at the defect level: the same defect in overlapping tiles or repeated
   frames, near-identical masks, and low variety in my own synthetic generator, checked both within the training set and across
   the split, because one physical defect in both training and test is a leak that image-level dedup misses. Then the
   distribution of defect sizes, contrasts and shapes, inconsistent or badly drawn
   masks, defect-centred sampling and rebalancing of rare defects, and a label-error workflow (confident learning ranks images for
   a person to review, tested on label noise I inject into the synthetic set). Injected noise is easier than real annotator error,
   and I found no labelled study of error rates in X-ray defect masks, so the post says what it cannot conclude. Again compared
   with a random control.
7. **Error analysis: reading the mistakes.** Sort every error into a small set of types (missed defect, false alarm, merged or
   split region, wrong boundary), with counts and example crops. The aim is a ranked list of what is going wrong, in the spirit of
   the error-analysis method from Part 4 of the Zero-to-Advanced series.
8. **Slice analysis: where does the model fail?** Slice by the generator's metadata (size, contrast, noise, thickness,
   background, count). Report worst-slice scores with counts and intervals, apply a minimum support, and confirm each finding on a
   second set. Say what multiple slices do to false alarms in the analysis itself.
9. **From analysis to a recommendation.** The decision the series is built around: more real data of a named kind, targeted
   synthetic data, curation (images or masks), a model or training change, label fixes, or nothing. A rule-based report goes first
   (slice table, train-versus-validation gap, a learning curve, a label-error estimate, perturbation results, mapped to actions by
   rules), then an agent writes the recommendation. New real data costs a person, so the factory produces a request with its
   evidence and a human approves.
10. **Try the fix: a data-poor slice gets synthetic data.** Take a slice that is bad because it has few examples, add targeted
    synthetic data, retrain and measure the **real** slice. Compare against plain augmentation with the same number of added
    examples and against doing nothing, vary how much synthetic data is added, and look for the point where more stops helping or
    starts hurting (the model learning synthetic artefacts). Report the result whichever way it goes.
11. **Round two: the loop again.** The next weakest slice, and a different kind of fix (curation, or a training or model change).
    Report the recommendation hit rate so far, and the rounds where the advice was wrong. On synthetic data, check whether the
    analysis recovers a cause I planted.
12. **The honest control: an equal-GPU-hour sweep.** The sweep against the agents, with LLM cost reported separately. If the sweep
    ties or wins in a fixed search space, the post says so.
13. **Agents that propose, run and judge experiments, on one shared GPU.** Recommendations feed the ticket queue, so the loop runs
    without me in it. Proposer, runner and judge are separate roles, the judge seeing only the gate's coarse verdict. The runner needs
    a scheduler for a machine shared with local model servers (memory estimates, admission control, OOM retry), and I have to measure
    this machine's memory behaviour first. Count wins on development data, wins that survive the confirmation set, and attempts to
    read protected paths from the audit log. Report all runs, not the best one.
14. **Measuring the false-win rate.** The A/A experiment and the replay of the main run's wins against the sealed set, with the
    definition above. The selection effect predicts that the best of many noisy runs looks better than it is (about 3 standard
    deviations for 100 runs, my own calculation), and correlated runs shrink that.
15. **The real-data check, and a retrospective.** A one-time local evaluation on real data with no images shown, what the
    synthetic-data results do and do not say about it, and what I would change.

The list may be trimmed or merged as I build. Posts 5 to 11 are the heart of the series.

## Constraints I will be upfront about

Everything runs on one GPU that is shared with other work, so scheduling is part of the design. Small test sets make small gains
unresolvable, and a post will say so instead of declaring a winner. A synthetic sealed set solves the size problem but not the
distribution-shift problem.

## How this series will be written

Same rules as the rest of the blog: every number comes from a real run, evaluation uses held-out data, each post ends with a
"what I did not do" section, and anything I could not run or verify is labelled as such.
